title: Time or Money: How to Book Calls People Actually Show Up To
summary: A training with new appointment setters. Yousif covers why ads alone don't make a business, why every client pays with time or money, why the owner has to call leads too, how to confirm and qualify without sounding like a salesperson, and how to build anticipation so booked calls show up.
content:
This episode comes from a training Yousif Alias ran for new appointment setters. It starts with what actually keeps a business alive, then gets practical: how to answer the "I'll just do it myself" objection, how to sound like a person on the phone, and how to book calls that people show up to.

Ads alone don't make a business

Results come from the whole thing working together: the ads, the AI, the follow-up systems, and someone calling the leads and building a relationship. Online videos tell people they just need AI. Yousif's list is longer: a registered business, a bank account, and enough money to stay in business for six to twelve months.

He has seen plenty of owners quit an industry after three months because that's all the money they had. He keeps a two-year runway. Staying in business is the part most people fail at.

Time or money

Nobody hands you success. You can walk business to business and prospect eight hours a day for free, or you can pay for ads and have clients come to you. "You can go and hunt for your food. It's free. But you can also DoorDash it for 20 bucks." That's how he answers the prospect who wants to do it all themselves.

The owner still has to show up

Some owners pay for marketing and expect the agency to do the closing too. Yousif doesn't buy it. If his sales team isn't calling, he calls the leads. If nobody is closing, he jumps in and closes. A team that watches the owner make money with or without them tends to work harder.

Sound like a person, not a script

He calls everyone 30 minutes before their appointment and keeps it light: "You got all your ducks in a row? You out of bed?" Robotic openers tell the prospect they're talking to a salesperson before you've said anything useful.

He role-plays a call with a Facebook lead. He mentions when the lead signed up, asks what kind of business they run, and then asks the questions himself: are you making sales, do you have a team, do you use a CRM, who does your books. You want to be the one qualifying them, not the one answering "yes sir, we do that."

Build anticipation before you book

Anybody can agree to an appointment. What gets them to show up is wanting to see what's on the other side. Yousif can often tell from a setter's recording whether a call will show. When the setter built real interest, the person shows and often closes fast.

Talk about the result, not the product. Ask where they are now and where they want to be. Ask if there's any reason they wouldn't make it. And when they push for price early, take it away: "Hold on, I don't think you should go with us yet. What's your sales process? Do you have anything set aside to invest?"

Do one thing for a long time

Yousif says there have been months when his agency spent more than all its revenue on ads. That's what it took. The alternative is becoming the person who does something new every year until nobody trusts them. Do one thing well for a long time and people come back.

title: Sales Fixes Everything: Train Your AI, Then Pick Up the Phone
summary: From a Saturday webinar. Yousif explains why an AI agent you set up and forget will fail and how he reviews every call it books to rewrite its prompt, why you always pay for clients with either money or time, why buyers of a business care about clients and recurring revenue more than leads, and why a sales focus beats content, funnels and likes.
content:
Six minutes from a Saturday webinar Yousif Alias ran for business owners. He covers how he trains his AI agent after every booked call, why you always pay for clients with money or with time, what a buyer looks at when they value your company, and why sales comes before content, funnels and likes.

The short version

  • 1. Train the agent like a new hire. Listen to the calls it books, write notes, and rewrite the prompt.
  • 2. Pick how you pay. Every client costs you money or time. Yousif chose money.
  • 3. Clients are what make a company worth something. Buyers ask about clients, monthly recurring revenue and profit, not your lead list.
  • 4. Sell first. Talk to customers. Everything else comes second.

An AI agent you set and forget will fail

Yousif listens to every call his AI agent books. He writes notes on each one, puts them on a single page, and hands that page to Claude with a plain request: give me a better prompt so the agent can handle a price objection, or give me a prompt so the agent confirms the call and the person actually shows up.

His rule is to treat the agent the way you would treat a new employee. You train a person, you teach them how you do things, and they get better. An agent won't teach itself. You go back into the prompt and make the edits.

You pay with money or with time

Getting clients always costs something. Yousif paid with his time for years and decided to stop, because paying for clients is simpler and faster. Compare how many business owners you would have to cold call to land one client with what a small ad budget brings in.

His point is that some people spend money to save time and others spend huge amounts of time to save money, then reach the end of the month with nothing to pay the bills.

Why breaking even on ads can still be a win

If you spend 10,000 on marketing and make 10,000 back, you still added clients, and clients are what raise the value of your company. When someone wants to buy a business, they don't ask about your leads. They ask how many clients you have, your monthly and annual recurring revenue, and your profit and loss.

Sales comes first

While everyone argues about which AI model to use, Yousif's advice is to go make sales: talk to customers and have personal conversations with them. He shares that his team once ran the wrong ad for nine months with a broken booking link and didn't notice, because they were busy calling leads and still closing deals.

He has also noticed that when he spends time posting and editing content, sales dip. Conversations with people come first, and the numbers, likes and views are noise.

title: Four Years at Zero: More Noes Than Yeses, and Doing One Thing
summary: From a team call. Yousif talks about the noes that outnumber the yeses in any sales job, why two days of calling proves nothing, the four years he made nothing while working as a dental assistant, in a nightclub and driving Uber to pay for ads, why working online takes more discipline, why his best clients do one thing, why the product has to be better than the sales team, and how AI changed the hardest part of leads.
keywords: how long until sales pay off
focus on one thing in business
content:
Four and a half minutes from a team call with new closers. Yousif Alias talks about the noes that come with any sales job, the four years he made nothing while paying for his own ads, why working from home takes more discipline, why his best clients do one thing, and why the product has to be better than the sales team.

The short version

  • 1. You will hear more noes than yeses. The yeses build the career, so don't let the noes stop you.
  • 2. Two days proves nothing. Yousif went four years before he earned a single dollar.
  • 3. Working from home is harder. Nobody is standing over you, so the work has to be self-driven.
  • 4. Do one thing well. His most successful clients stick to their one skill and hand off the rest.
  • 5. The product sells the company. Clients from 2016 still pay because the work gets results.

More noes than yeses

Yousif says that if someone had told him on day one how many people would say no, he probably would have quit before he started. In any sales job, insurance included, the noes outnumber the yeses. The yeses are what build your career, and each no gets you one step closer to the next yes.

A new closer messaged him after two days of calls with no deal. Yousif told him he did this for four years before he got paid. You build a relationship with a lead over time. Calling someone and asking "want to buy these ads?" in the first ten seconds gets a no from everybody.

Dental assistant, nightclub, Uber

Those first four years were hard. Yousif worked as a dental assistant during the day, worked a nightclub shift at night, and drove Uber after that, all to pay for ads and learn how to run them properly. He paid one so-called mentor 10K to teach him, and that person didn't even show up to teach. He hired other people to do it.

Working from home is the hard version

Online work looks easy because you don't drive anywhere or burn gas, and you aren't out in the field. Yousif's view is the opposite. Since nobody is there to make you pick up the phone, you have to tell yourself you're going to sit down and do the work, and then do it.

Your best clients do one thing

The pattern he sees in his successful clients is focus. A CPA does CPA work. He doesn't want to run his own marketing or do his own closings. Yousif runs his own work the same way: he does ads, and he doesn't want to do SEO, organic content or anything else.

He's also honest that his company has never had the best sales team. What keeps it going is a product that gets people results, so clients from 2016 are still paying and referrals keep coming in. If the product is good, it sells itself.

The hardest part of leads got easier

Generating leads is the easy part. Getting someone to call them is hard. AI has made that part easier. On the day of this call, his AI setter had already booked three appointments on his calendar.

This episode stays on the mindset. The day-to-day side, the calls and the setups behind them, is what Yousif teaches inside Freedom Club.
